questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying Expressions in Degrees Using the Sum and Difference Formulas
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the sum formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v={120}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+{120}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡{120}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡{120}^{∘} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Geometric Interpretation of the Roots of Unity
questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams shows all the $5$th roots of unity?
questions.worked_solution:
Geometrically, the $5$th roots of unity have the following properties:

- all of them lie on the unit circle centered in the origin,

- one of the roots is $1,$ corresponding to the point $(1,0)$ on the complex plane,

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation
questions.problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-4t,\,\,\,y={t}^{2}-1,\,t\le 0,
$$

what is the range of $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the range of $x,$ note that $x=1-4t\ge 1$ for all $t\le 0.$ 

Consequently, the range of $x$ is $x\ge 1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=-1$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{x}^{2}+2x+1}{({x}^{2}-4)^{2}-12x-21} & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{[{x}^{2}+2x+1]}^{′}}{{[({x}^{2}-4)^{2}-12x-21]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{2x+2}{4x({x}^{2}-4)-12} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{x+1}{2x({x}^{2}-4)-6}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{x}^{2}+2x+1}{({x}^{2}-4)^{2}-12x-21} & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{x+1}{2x({x}^{2}-4)-6} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{{[x+1]}^{′}}{{[2x({x}^{2}-4)-6]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{1}{6{x}^{2}-8} \\  & =\frac{1}{6(-1)^{2}-8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Solutions to First-Order Differential Equations
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{5y}{x},\,x\ne 0.
$$

 Which of the following is a solution to this equation?

- $y={x}^{5}$
- $y={x}^{10}$
- $y=5{x}^{4}$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a solution to a differential equation, it must satisfy the equation for all values of $x$ in the equation's domain.

We check each proposed solution by differentiating and substituting it into the original equation. 

- Differentiating $y={x}^{5},$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=5{x}^{4}.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{5y}{x} \\ 5{x}^{4} & \overset{?}{=}\frac{5({x}^{5})}{x} \\ 5{x}^{4} & =5{x}^{4}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *true*. Therefore, the function $y={x}^{5}$ *is* a solution to our differential equation.

- Differentiating $y={x}^{10},$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=10{x}^{9}.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{5y}{x} \\ 10{x}^{9} & \overset{?}{=}\frac{5({x}^{10})}{x} \\ 10{x}^{9} & \overset{?}{=}5{x}^{9} \\ 5{x}^{9} & \ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *not true* for all $x.$ Therefore, the function $y={x}^{10}$ is *not* a solution to our differential equation.

- Differentiating $y=5{x}^{4},$ we get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=20{x}^{3}.$ Substituting into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{5y}{x} \\ 20{x}^{3} & \overset{?}{=}\frac{5(5{x}^{4})}{x} \\ 20{x}^{3} & \overset{?}{=}25{x}^{3} \\ 0 & \ne 5{x}^{3}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

This statement is *not true* for all $x.$ Therefore, the function $y=5{x}^{4}$ is *not* a solution to our differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components
questions.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,q\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}+{q}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 1+4\cdot 1+2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{4}} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{p}\,q & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,p\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{p}_{x}^{2}+{p}_{y}^{2}+{p}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}+(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{25}} \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p+{\text{comp}}_{p}\,q & =\frac{9}{2}+\frac{9}{5} \\  & =9(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =9(\frac{5}{10}+\frac{2}{10}) \\  & =\frac{63}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Scalar Projection Using Components

questions.knowledge_point: Solving for an Unknown Given the Determinant
questions.problem: Find the possible values of the constant $x$ given that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ x & -1 & -x\end{aligned}]$ is singular.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's use our formula to find an expression for the determinant in terms of $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ x & -1 & -x\end{aligned}| & =3|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -x\end{aligned}|-5|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ x & -x\end{aligned}|+8|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ x & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(-x+2)-5(-x-2x)+8(-1-x) \\  & =-3x+6+15x-8-8x \\  & =4x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix is singular, the determinant is $0,$ and we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-2 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\frac{1}{2}.$

provenance.kp_title: Solving for an Unknown Given the Determinant
